overview: Two forms of nuclear division with very different purposes: one keeps cells identical, the other creates genetic diversity for reproduction.
genZNote: Mitosis: same energy, new copy. Meiosis: shuffle the deck, deal half a hand.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Nuclear division producing two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, used for growth and repair.
aspects.valueB: Two rounds of division producing four genetically unique haploid daughter cells, used for sexual reproduction.

aspects.label: Number of Divisions
aspects.valueB: Two divisions (Meiosis I and Meiosis II) from a single round of DNA replication.

aspects.label: Daughter Cell Number and Ploidy
aspects.valueA: Two diploid (2n) cells, genetically identical to the parent.
aspects.valueB: Four haploid (n) cells, each genetically distinct.

aspects.label: Genetic Variation
aspects.valueA: None introduced — daughter cells are clones of the parent cell.
aspects.valueB: Introduced via crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment (metaphase I).

aspects.label: Homologous Chromosome Pairing
aspects.valueA: Does not occur — chromosomes act independently.
aspects.valueB: Homologous chromosomes pair up as tetrads during prophase I, enabling crossing over.

aspects.label: Biological Context
aspects.valueA: Somatic cell division: growth, tissue repair, asexual reproduction in some organisms.
aspects.valueB: Germ cell division: production of gametes (sperm and egg) for sexual reproduction.

aspects.label: Limitations / Pitfalls
aspects.valueA: Errors (nondisjunction) are rare but can contribute to cancer if checkpoints fail.
aspects.valueB: Errors in chromosome segregation (nondisjunction) cause aneuploidies such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: One division, two identical diploid cells, no crossing over.
aspects.valueB: Two divisions, four unique haploid cells, crossing over and independent assortment.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Crossing over happens in prophase I of meiosis only — never in mitosis.
overlay.commonMisconception: Meiosis does not happen in every cell — only in germline cells destined to become gametes.
